Eggs of the Barnacle goose Branta leucopsis are incubated at a mean temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that supports embryonic development over an average period of 25 days [ab = 25 days]. Newly hatched goslings emerge at a relatively modest wet weight of 60 grams [Wwb = 60 grams], a value that reflects the substantial yolk reserves that must be metabolised during the final stages of incubation. This neonatal mass is consistent with the semi-precocial developmental mode typical of the genus Branta, in which chicks are capable of leaving the nest within hours of hatching and begin foraging independently almost immediately. The combination of a precise incubation temperature and a short developmental period likely represents an adaptation to the short Arctic summers in which this species breeds, where any delay in hatching could compromise the timing of subsequent life-history events such as fledging and southward migration.

Goslings grow rapidly after hatching, and the transitional stage of fledging is generally attained at 42 days [tx = 42 days] after emergence from the egg. This interval marks the point at which the juvenile flight feathers have fully developed, enabling sustained flight and reducing vulnerability to terrestrial predators. The timing of fledging is tightly constrained by the polar growing season; a delay beyond 42 days could expose the young to harsh autumn conditions before they have acquired the necessary flight skills and fat reserves for migration. Field records from Svalbard and the Baltic Sea indicate that most goslings achieve this milestone within the expected window, though local variation in food availability can cause slight deviations. The synchrony of fledging with the general population is crucial because young geese that fledge later in the season often have reduced survival rates during their first autumn migration to the wintering grounds in northern Europe.

Sexual maturity in Barnacle geese is not reached until well after the fledging period, with puberty occurring at 126 days after hatching [tp = 126 days after hatching]. This relatively delayed onset of gonadal activation is typical of long-lived waterfowl that invest heavily in early somatic growth and feather development before any reproductive effort is initiated. Young birds spend their first autumn and winter consuming high-energy grasses and sedges to build the body condition necessary for future breeding attempts. The 126-day interval to puberty aligns with the end of the post-fledging period, when juvenile birds have attained skeletal maturity and are beginning to integrate into winter flocks. It is important to note, however, that achieving puberty does not equate to immediate breeding; many individuals defer their first actual nesting attempt for an additional year or more as they continue to refine foraging skills and establish pair bonds within the flock hierarchy.

The onset of first reproduction in Barnacle geese is significantly delayed relative to puberty, with the first brood typically being produced at 2 years after hatching [tR = 2 years after hatching]. This deferred reproductive schedule is common among Arctic-nesting geese, where the energetic demands of egg production, incubation, and brood rearing are substantial and require a well-developed body frame and ample fat stores. Females generally do not attain the necessary body mass until their second year, and even then, only a subset of the population breeds successfully in any given season. The annual reproductive output of an adult female is modest; each clutch contains a small number of eggs, and a female typically produces only one clutch per breeding season. When expressed across the entire year, this translates to a maximum reproductive rate of 1.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1.5 eggs per clutch] and approximately 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch per year], a low annual investment that underscores the species' slow life-history pace.

Adult Barnacle geese exhibit pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males attaining a greater ultimate wet weight than females. Females typically reach a maximum adult body mass of 1586 grams [Wwi = 1586 grams], whereas males average 1788 grams [Wwi = 1788 grams] at full maturity, representing a size advantage of roughly 13 percent. Both sexes begin life with an initial wet weight of 104 grams [Ww0 = 104 grams] at the moment of hatching, reflecting the mass of the hatchling immediately after emergence and before any exogenous feeding has occurred. This starting mass provides the baseline from which the rapid growth trajectory of the first weeks is measured. The maximum longevity recorded for this species in the wild is approximately 28.2 years [am = approximately 28.2 years], a lifespan that is among the highest documented for any goose species and that allows multiple reproductive attempts over a lifetime despite the low annual fecundity.
